title: Photonic Cluster State Generation from a Quantum Dot Emitting in the Telecom C-band
authors: Giora Peniakov, Reza Hekmati, Johannes Michl, Mohamed Helal, Moritz Meinecke, Jochen Kaupp, Yorick Reum, Martin Kamp, Monika Emmerling, Andreas Theo Pfenning, Sven Hoefling, Tobias Huber-Loyola
abstract: Photonic cluster states are a key resource for photonic quantum information processing. So far, deterministic generation of these states has been limited to the near-infrared wavelength range. To achieve quantum advantage in communication while maintaining compatibility with silicon photonics, operation in the telecom wavelength range is required. In this work, we demonstrate deterministic cluster state generation directly in the telecom C-band. This is achieved through repetitive excitation of a hole spin confined in an indium-arsenide quantum dot subjected to an external magnetic field. We characterize the quantum process that generates the cluster state by measuring its process map, obtaining a fidelity of $\mathrm{F} = 0.71 \pm 0.01$ to the ideal case. As part of this characterization, we observe spin--photon polarization entanglement with a negativity of $\mathrm{N} = 0.27 \pm 0.02$. The emitted photons exhibit indistinguishability of at least 83%, demonstrating the potential for future fusion gates necessary for photonic cluster state generation beyond linear connectivity.
summary: The research demonstrates deterministic cluster state generation using an indium-arsenide quantum dot operating at the telecom C-band. By characterizing the underlying quantum process map and measuring spin-photon entanglement, the authors confirm the feasibility of creating multi-qubit entangled states necessary for scalable photonic quantum computation.
main_problem: The primary goal is the deterministic generation of photonic cluster states directly within the telecom C-band (1549 nm) to enable quantum communication compatible with existing fiber infrastructure.
main_result: The authors successfully demonstrated this process, achieving a measured process map fidelity ($\mathcal{F}$) of $0.71 \pm 0.01$ and generating a state locally equivalent to a three-qubit cluster state (GHZ state).
method: Cluster state generation is achieved using a quantum dot system that implements controlled gates via hole spin excitation, followed by full characterization using process tomography.
model_or_system: The platform utilizes an Indium-arsenide ($	ext{InAs}$) quantum dot embedded in a microcavity. The protocol relies on manipulating the hole spin state to mediate entanglement between the spin and emitted photon, following variants of the Lindner–Rudolph protocol.
key_observables: Process map fidelity ($\mathcal{F} = 0.71 \pm 0.01$), spin–photon polarization entanglement negativity ($\mathcal{N} = 0.27 \pm 0.02$), and photon indistinguishability (at least 83%).
important_parameters: Telecom C-band wavelength (1549 nm), hole-spin coherence time ($T_2^* = 15.9 \pm 1.7$ ns), and high repetition rate (80 MHz).
main_assumptions: The protocol assumes that characterizing a single Circuit Building Block (CBB) is sufficient to characterize $N$ qubits by concatenation, and it relies on spectral detuning compensated by Purcell enhancement.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the microcavity setup, pulse sequences for spin state characterization, tomography results showing entanglement quantification ($\mathcal{N}$), and comparisons between measured and ideal process maps ($\Phi$).
paper_structure: The paper details the physical system and protocol (using hole spins in a QD) to generate cluster states. It then presents rigorous characterization methods—including process map reconstruction, entanglement measurement via tomography, and indistinguishability tests—culminating in the demonstration of a multi-qubit state.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses a major engineering bottleneck in quantum networking by achieving high-fidelity photonic entanglement generation at telecom wavelengths using solid-state emitters, which is crucial for scaling up quantum communication networks.
